terms.grammar: pronoun and adjective; gen. utriusque, dat. utrīque; with a singular verb
evidence: Plin. Ep. 4.1.1: grātum est utrīque nostrum
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: uterque takes the two one by one, ambō as a pair. With a noun it agrees; with a pronoun it takes a genitive: uterque nostrum, both of us. A plural verb with it is rare in the best prose, never in Cicero (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: numeral adjective, declined like duo: dat. and abl. ambōbus, ambābus
evidence: Plaut. Rud. 1423: vōs hīc hodiē cēnātōte ambō
Catull. 104.2: ambōbus mihi quae cārior est oculīs
terms.comment: The masculine accusative is ambō in Cicero, Caesar, Vergil and Horace, who never write ambōs (Lewis & Short); Livy has ambōs (1.55.1).

phrases.latin: Albānum … sīve Falernum tē magis adpositīs dēlectat, habēmus utrumque
phrases.english: if you like Alban or Falernian better than what is on the table, we have both

phrases.latin: grātum est utrīque nostrum quod cupis
phrases.english: your wish is welcome to both of us

phrases.latin: vōs hīc hodiē cēnātōte ambō. — Fīat.
phrases.english: you’re both to dine here today. — Done.

phrases.latin: amplexus ille utrumque et carpēns ōscula dulcemque in ambōs cāritātem partiēns
phrases.english: he hugged them both, kissing them and sharing his tender love between the two

phrases.latin: crēdis mē potuisse meae maledīcere vītae, ambōbus mihi quae cārior est oculīs?
phrases.english: do you think I could have spoken ill of my life, who is dearer to me than both my eyes?

phrases.latin: hic quidem ait nōs eandem crisin habēre, quia utrīque dentēs cadunt
phrases.english: he says that we have reached the same turning point, because both of us are losing our teeth
